newsitem.title: ROMANIA: On the sidelines of Clinton's visit to Romania.
newsitem.headline: On the sidelines of Clinton's visit to Romania.

text.p: Following is a collection of off-beat notes and quotes associated with U.S. President Bill Clinton's one-day visit to Romania:
Clinton used the image of one of Romania's popular sports figures, New York women's marathon winner Anuta Catuna, to illustrate how impressed he was with Romania's efforts to introduce tough reforms.

"At the end of the New York marathon last year, a runner named Anuta Catuna came from behind to take the lead and earned her way to victory in one of America's most prized races," he told tens of thousands in Bucharest's University Square.

"Like her, Romania has set is sights and its heart on the long run and like her, the Romanian people have won the world's respect for moving so far, so fast and for believing in yourselves and your future."
The dimunitive Catuna, 30, won $50,000 for her victory last year in New York. She is now preparing for next month's world athletics championship in Greece.

An association grouping veterans of Romania's December 1989 anti-communist uprising had planned to present Clinton with a diploma honouring him as a "universal hooligan" after his address to crowds in University Square.
The Square is the traditional site for protests and celebrations. Former leftist president Ion Iliescu branded students demonstrating there against him in 1990 as hooligans.
The students were eventually dispersed in June 1990 by vigilante miners armed with clubs. Iliescu was voted out of office last November.
It was unknown whether Clinton received the diploma.

But Petre Roman, Romania's first post-Communist prime minister who took part in the upheaval, handed Clinton a Romanian red, yellow and blue tricolor with a hole in the centre as he completed his address. The flag, with its communist crest torn from the centre by protesters became the symbol of the revolt.
The daily Adevarul said Bucharest's Health Department issued an order last Monday "forbidding pyschiatric hospitals to release patients from July 9-11," coinciding with Clinton's visit.

Adevarul said doctors told to implement the order "were appalled. Hospitals of all types in Bucharest received the order and doctors said it was unacceptable to keep patients for any period longer than necessary."

The newspaper said that in 1984, when Romania was under communist rule, similar instructions were issued during the University Games in Bucharest. They went further, ordering Romanians with a history of psychiatric problems to be admitted to hospitals wherever they might be.

Leontina Diaconescu, a Romanian specialist in metapsychology, the study of the link between mind and body and, more particularly, of each human being's previous lives, says President Clinton has a Russian connection.
"In his previous life, Clinton was born a woman in 1425 in Siberia," Diaconescu told the daily National.
"She was the wife of a cattle breeder and worked very hard. She looked after the house and the children and rode wildly through the taiga."

In his previous incarnation, Clinton grew tired of a drunken husband and beat him relentlessly, she said. "That is why in his reincarnation, Clinton has proven to be a man full of energy, willing to learn anything, ready to conquer the entire world."

With Bucharest's main thoroughfares blocked off 24 hours before the president's arrival and tough security measures in operation, Romania's SRI intelligence service and the U.S. FBI worked together to keep Clinton safe.

Trains on Bucharest's underground sped without stopping through Piata Universitatii station beneath the square where Clinton spoke. But Bucharest dailies said each carriage still carried two agents -- one from each intelligence service.

The Romanian SRI is still widely viewed, seven years after the fall of communism, as being linked to late dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's dreaded Securitate force, whose vast network intimidated most ordinary Romanians.
